As at 2026-11-06, under the Active Mobility Act 2017 (Singapore), a cyclist may lawfully ride on a pedestrian-only path under certain circumstances:

1. Crossing by the shortest safe route: A cyclist may ride on a pedestrian-only path if they are crossing it by the shortest safe route and do not stay on the path longer than necessary to cross it safely [CITE:1(2)(a)(i)].

2. Obstruction on adjacent area: A cyclist may ride on a pedestrian-only path if there is an obstruction on a road, footpath, or shared path adjacent to the pedestrian-only path, it is impracticable to travel on the adjacent area, and the cyclist travels no more than reasonably necessary along the pedestrian-only path to avoid the obstruction [CITE:1(2)(b)(i), (ii), (iii)].

3. Employment-related activities: A cyclist may ride on a pedestrian-only path if they are driving a mechanized sweeper on the path in the course of their employment, which is to sweep or otherwise clean sidewalks or paths [CITE:1(3)].

It is important to note that these exceptions do not apply to all cyclists or all pedestrian-only paths, and the cyclist must still comply with other provisions of the Act, such as not riding recklessly or in a manner dangerous to the public [CITE:4(1)].

As at 2026-11-06, the use of a mobile communication device while riding an e-scooter along a footpath in Singapore is regulated by the Active Mobility Act 2017 and the Road Traffic Act 1961. 

Under section 22A of the Active Mobility Act 2017, a rider of a vehicle, including an e-scooter, must not hold in their hand a mobile communication device and operate any of its communication or other functions when the vehicle is moving on a public path [CITE:1]. This section does not apply to a mobile communication device that is a wearable device, such as a smart watch, when it is worn by the driver or rider in the manner intended by the manufacturer of the wearable device [CITE:1].

Similarly, section 65B of the Road Traffic Act 1961 prohibits a driver of a vehicle from holding in their hand a mobile communication device and operating any of its communicative or other functions while the vehicle is in motion on a road or in a public place. This section also does not apply to a mobile communication device that is a wearable device, such as a smart watch, when it is worn by the driver or rider in the manner intended by the manufacturer of the wearable device [CITE:5].

Therefore, if you are riding an e-scooter along a footpath and using a smart watch that is worn in the manner intended by the manufacturer, you would not be in breach of these provisions. However, if you are using a handheld mobile communication device, you would be contravening the law.

As at 2026-11-06, the maximum penalty under the Active Mobility Act 2017 for a repeat offender who exceeds the speed limit on a footpath or shared path is a fine not exceeding $5,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or to both [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, under the Active Mobility Act 2017 (Singapore), section 23A provides that an individual commits an offence if they ride a motorised personal mobility device on a shared path when they are below the prescribed minimum riding age for that device on the shared path [CITE:1]. However, subsection (3) of section 23A states that this provision does not apply where the individual riding the motorised personal mobility device on a shared path is riding under escort by one or more appropriate supervisors, whether or not a parent or guardian [CITE:1].

Therefore, if a young child who is below the minimum age for riding a motorised scooter on a shared path is riding under the escort of an adult, they may do so without committing an offence. The term "riding under escort" is defined in section 23A(4) to mean having an appropriate supervisor on or in the vicinity of the shared path when the under-aged rider is riding, and riding in such a way that the supervisor has a clear and unobstructed line of sight of the rider [CITE:1].

It is important to note that the specific minimum riding age for motorised personal mobility devices on shared paths may be prescribed by regulations under the Act [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, the Active Mobility Act 2017 (Singapore) provides that an individual must not ride an unregistered registrable personal mobility device on any footpath or shared path, knowing that, or reckless as to whether, the registrable personal mobility device is unregistered [CITE:1]. This provision is found in section 28B of the Act, which falls under PART 3 USE OF PUBLIC PATHS, Division 4 - Wayfinding and maintaining clear public paths. Riding an unregistered registrable personal mobility device in violation of this section constitutes an offence, and upon conviction, the individual may be liable to a fine not exceeding $2,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 months, or both [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, the law in Singapore does not recognize an agreement between a driver and a passenger to exclude the driver's liability for an accident as enforceable. This is based on the provisions of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960, specifically section 5 [CITE:2].

Section 5(1) of the Act states that any antecedent agreement or understanding between a person using a motor vehicle and any other person carried in or upon the vehicle is of no effect to the extent that it purports to negate or restrict the driver's liability for the persons carried in or upon the vehicle. This means that an agreement made before an accident occurs, where the passenger agrees not to hold the driver liable, is not legally binding and does not protect the driver from liability that must be insured under the Act.

Furthermore, section 5(2) of the Act clarifies that the fact that a passenger has willingly accepted the risk of negligence on the part of the driver does not negate the driver's liability. This reinforces the principle that the driver's insurance obligations cannot be waived by an agreement with the passenger.

In summary, an agreement between a driver and a passenger to exclude the driver's liability for an accident does not protect the driver from the legal obligations imposed by the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960. The driver is still required to maintain insurance coverage as required by the Act, and any agreement to the contrary is unenforceable.

judge_note: States s 7 correctly but then suggests unrelated exceptions (Parks and Trees Act, case law), muddying the answer
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the question of whether you can make the Government pay for damage to your car while parked in a public car park managed by the authorities is governed by several legal principles and provisions.

Firstly, under the Parking Places Act 1974, section 7 states that the exercise of powers under the Act by the Authority or the Superintendent does not render the Government, the Authority, or the Superintendent subject to any liability for loss or damage to any vehicle or its contents parked in such a parking place [CITE:1]. This suggests that the Government may not be liable for damage to your vehicle while parked in a public car park.

However, there are exceptions to this general rule. For instance, the Parks and Trees Act 2005, section 47 provides that in court proceedings for an offence under the Act that relates to damaged or destroyed property owned by the Government or the Board, the court may make an order requiring the person convicted to pay to the Government or the Board a sum representing the value of the damaged property [CITE:2]. This indicates that if the damage to your car is a result of an offence under the Parks and Trees Act 2005, you may seek compensation from the Government.

Additionally, the Parks and Trees Act 2005, section 42B allows for the immediate removal of dangerous or obstructing vehicles in national parks, nature reserves, or public parks. If your vehicle was removed due to being dangerous or obstructing, and this action caused damage, you may have grounds to seek compensation [CITE:3].

The Road Traffic Act 1961, section 97 also addresses certain situations where liability may arise, such as when a person takes hold of a motor vehicle in motion without lawful authority or reasonable cause, or when a person loiters in or near a road or parking place for the purpose of importuning [CITE:4]. However, these provisions do not directly address the scenario of damage to a parked vehicle.

In the context of negligence, the case of Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No 2668 v Rott George Hugo [2013] SGHC 114 illustrates that occupiers of property, such as a car park, owe a duty of care to lawful entrants. If the occupier breaches this duty of care and causes damage to a vehicle parked in the car park, the occupier may be liable for negligence [CITE:10][CITE:11][CITE:16].

In summary, while the Government may not generally be liable for damage to your car while parked in a public car park, there are exceptions where liability may arise depending on the circumstances of the damage and the relevant legal provisions. If you believe your car has been damaged due to the negligence of the authorities or due to an offence under the Parks and Trees Act 2005, you may seek compensation. However, it is important to note that the availability of compensation would depend on the specific facts and circumstances of your case.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Parking Places Act 1974, the owner of a vehicle may avoid liability for a parking offence committed with that vehicle under certain circumstances. These are outlined in section 14 of the Act:

1. **Stolen or Illegally Taken Vehicle**: The owner may avoid liability if they can satisfy the Superintendent or the court that the vehicle was at the relevant time a stolen vehicle or a vehicle illegally taken or used [CITE:1].

2. **Statutory Declaration**: The owner must, within 14 days after service of a notice alleging the offence, furnish a statutory declaration to the Superintendent with the name and address of the person who was in charge of the vehicle at all relevant times relating to the parking offence [CITE:1].

3. **Lack of Knowledge**: The owner must satisfy the Superintendent or the court that they did not know and could not with reasonable diligence have ascertained the name and address of the person in charge of the vehicle [CITE:1].

4. **Prima Facie Evidence**: A statutory declaration made under this subsection is prima facie evidence that the person named was in charge of the vehicle at all relevant times relating to the parking offence [CITE:1].

These provisions provide the owner with a mechanism to establish that they were not responsible for the parking offence, thereby avoiding liability. However, it is important to note that the onus is on the owner to prove these circumstances.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Parking Places Act 1974, a driver may not ply for hire or accept passengers for hire inside a parking place that has not been appointed a public stand under section 109 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 [CITE:1]. This prohibition is outlined in section 10 of the Parking Places Act 1974 [CITE:1]. Any person who contravenes this section commits an offence [CITE:1].

3. A circumstance prescribed in the regulations applies at the time of import [CITE:1(2)(c)].

These provisions are outlined in Section 5 of the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Act 2020 [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, under the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Act 2020 (Singapore), a person needs the following to import a small motorised vehicle:

1. **Import Approval**: The person must be granted an import approval for the small motorised vehicle [CITE:2].
2. **Authorisation**: The person must be authorised, in writing, by the person who is granted the import approval to import the vehicle [CITE:2].

As at 2026-11-06, the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1972 (Singapore) does not imply an absolute undertaking by the carrier to provide a seaworthy ship. Section 4 of the Act explicitly states that there shall not be implied in any contract for the carriage of goods by sea to which the Rules apply any absolute undertaking by the carrier of the goods to provide a seaworthy ship [CITE:1]. This provision overrides any common law or equitable principles that might suggest an absolute warranty of seaworthiness.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1972 (Singapore), the International Convention for the unification of certain rules of law relating to bills of lading, made at Brussels on 25 August 1924, as amended by the Protocol made at Brussels on 23 February 1968, has the force of law in Singapore [CITE:1]. This convention, commonly known as the Hague Rules, is set out in the Schedule to the Act and forms the basis of the law governing bills of lading in Singapore.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Bills of Lading Act 1992 (Singapore), a person who becomes the lawful holder of a bill of lading acquires certain rights and liabilities. These rights are as follows:

1. **Rights of Suit under the Contract of Carriage**: A person who becomes the lawful holder of a bill of lading, or who is to receive delivery of goods under a sea waybill or a ship's delivery order, shall have transferred to and vested in him all rights of suit under the contract of carriage as if he had been a party to that contract [CITE:1(1)].

2. **Liabilities under the Contract of Carriage**: If the person takes or demands delivery from the carrier, makes a claim under the contract of carriage, or was previously entitled to delivery, they become subject to the same liabilities under that contract as if they had been a party to it [CITE:3(1)].

3. **Conclusive Evidence**: A bill of lading, when signed by the master of the vessel or a person with authority to sign, is conclusive evidence against the carrier of the shipment or receipt for shipment of the goods [CITE:2].

4. **Rights for the Benefit of the Person Who Sustained Loss or Damage**: If a person sustains loss or damage due to a breach of the contract of carriage and rights of suit are vested in another person, the other person shall be entitled to exercise those rights for the benefit of the person who sustained the loss or damage [CITE:1(4)].

These rights are subject to the provisions of the Act and the terms of the bill of lading itself. It is important to note that the rights and liabilities are not absolute and are subject to the terms and conditions of the contract of carriage and the provisions of the Act.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Bills of Lading Act 1992 (Singapore), the holder of a bill of lading becomes subject to liabilities under the contract of carriage in certain circumstances:

1. **Taking or Demanding Delivery**: If the holder takes or demands delivery from the carrier of any of the goods to which the document relates [CITE:1(1)(a)].

2. **Making a Claim**: If the holder makes a claim under the contract of carriage against the carrier in respect of any of those goods [CITE:1(1)(b)].

3. **Prior Delivery**: If the holder, before rights were vested in them, took or demanded delivery from the carrier of any of those goods [CITE:1(1)(c)].

This means that once a person assumes the role of a holder by engaging in these actions, they become liable under the contract of carriage as if they had been a party to that contract from the outset [CITE:1(1)].

As at 2026-11-06, under the Bills of Lading Act 1992 (Singapore), section 4 provides that a bill of lading which represents goods to have been shipped on board a vessel or received for shipment on board a vessel, and has been signed by the master of the vessel or a person with the authority to sign bills of lading, shall be conclusive evidence against the carrier of the shipment of the goods or their receipt for shipment [CITE:1]. This means that once a bill of lading is issued and signed by the appropriate authority, the carrier cannot later deny that the goods were shipped.

However, there are exceptions to this rule. For instance, under the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1972 (Singapore), section 6 provides that the carrier and the ship shall not be entitled to the benefit of certain limitations of liability if the damage resulted from an act or omission of the carrier done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result [CITE:2]. Additionally, if the nature or value of the goods has been knowingly mis-stated by the shipper in the bill of lading, the carrier shall not be responsible for loss or damage to the goods [CITE:2].

It is also important to note that the Merchant Shipping Act 1995 (Singapore) contains provisions that may affect the rights and obligations of carriers and shippers. For example, section 92 requires a person ceasing to be the master of a ship to deliver to their successor the documents relating to the ship or its crew which are in their custody [CITE:5]. Furthermore, section 94 grants the master of any ship the power to cause any person on board to be put under restraint if necessary for the interest of safety or for the preservation of good order or discipline on board the ship [CITE:6].

In summary, while a shipping document signed by the ship's master is generally conclusive evidence that the goods were shipped, there are exceptions and other legal provisions that may affect the carrier's liability.

As at 2026-11-06, a contract of marine insurance is deemed to be a gaming or wagering contract under the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (Singapore) under the following circumstances:

1. Where the assured has not an insurable interest as defined by the Act, and the contract is entered into with no expectation of acquiring such an interest [CITE:1].
2. Where the policy is made "interest or no interest", or "without further proof of interest than the policy itself", or "without benefit of salvage to the insurer", or subject to any other like term [CITE:1].

These provisions are part of Section 4 of the Marine Insurance Act 1906, which outlines the conditions under which a marine insurance contract is considered void due to its nature as a gaming or wagering contract.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (Singapore), the assured must disclose to the insurer, before the contract is concluded, every material circumstance which is known to the assured. This includes circumstances that the assured is deemed to know, which would influence the judgment of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium or determining whether to take the risk [CITE:1]. The assured is also deemed to know every circumstance which, in the ordinary course of business, ought to be known by him [CITE:1]. If the assured fails to make such disclosure, the insurer may avoid the contract [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, if one side to a ship insurance contract is not completely honest with the other, the contract may be subject to cancellation or avoidance, depending on the nature of the dishonesty and the provisions of the contract itself.

Under the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (Singapore), section 17 states that a contract of marine insurance is a contract based upon the utmost good faith [CITE:5]. This principle is known as uberrimae fidei. If the utmost good faith is not observed by either party, the contract may be avoided by the other party [CITE:5]. This means that if one party provides false or misleading information, or withholds material information, the other party may have grounds to cancel the contract.

The Micro Tellers Network Limited & 3 Ors v Cheng Yi Han (Zhong Yihan) & 4 Ors [2023] SGHC(I) 13 case illustrates the application of this principle. The court held that where there is dishonest assistance in a breach of trust, the standard of what constitutes honest conduct is an objective one. If the defendant had such knowledge of the irregular shortcomings of the transaction that ordinary honest people would consider it to be a breach of standards of honest conduct if he failed to adequately query them, then the assistance is dishonest [CITE:6,16].

However, the ability to cancel the contract due to dishonesty would also depend on the specific terms of the insurance contract. For instance, the Marine Insurance Act 1906, section 84 provides for the return of the premium in certain circumstances, including where the consideration for the payment of the premium totally fails, and there has been no fraud or illegality on the part of the assured or his agents [CITE:10].

In summary, while the principle of utmost good faith in marine insurance contracts allows for the possibility of cancellation or avoidance in cases of dishonesty, the specific circumstances and the terms of the contract would determine whether such action is permissible. It is advisable to consult the specific contract and legal advice for a definitive determination in any given case.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (Singapore), in a voyage policy, there is an implied warranty that at the commencement of the voyage, the ship shall be seaworthy for the purpose of the particular adventure insured [CITE:1]. This warranty extends to situations where the policy attaches while the ship is in port, implying that she shall, at the commencement of the risk, be reasonably fit to encounter the ordinary perils of the port [CITE:1].

A ship is deemed to be seaworthy when she is reasonably fit in all respects to encounter the ordinary perils of the seas of the adventure insured [CITE:1]. This implies that the ship must be in a condition that allows her to safely navigate the seas and face the expected risks of the voyage.

As at 2026-11-06, if an insured ship deviates from its planned route without a good reason but returns to it before anything goes wrong, the insurer is discharged from liability as from the time of deviation, according to section 46 of the Marine Insurance Act 1906 [CITE:1]. This means that if a loss occurs after the deviation, the insurer is not required to pay for that loss. The fact that the ship may have regained its original route before any loss occurs is immaterial to the insurer's liability.

answer:
As at 2026-11-06, under the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (Singapore), if an insured ship goes missing and no news of her has been received after a reasonable time, the assured may be able to claim for an actual total loss without the need to give notice of abandonment. This is in accordance with section 58 of the Act, which states that where the ship concerned in the adventure is missing, and after the lapse of a reasonable time no news of her has been received, an actual total loss may be presumed [CITE:1].

However, it is important to note that the Act does not explicitly state that notice of abandonment is not required in such a scenario. Section 60 of the Act defines constructive total loss, which includes situations where the subject-matter insured is reasonably abandoned on account of its actual total loss appearing to be unavoidable [CITE:8]. This suggests that while notice of abandonment may not be a strict requirement for claiming an actual total loss due to the ship's disappearance, the principles surrounding abandonment and notice may still be relevant in practice.

Therefore, while the Act does not mandate the giving of notice of abandonment in the specific situation of a missing ship, it is advisable for the assured to consult the policy terms and seek legal advice to ensure compliance with the policy's requirements and the Act's provisions.

As at 2026-11-06, a constructive total loss under the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (Singapore) is defined in section 60 of the Act. A constructive total loss occurs where the subject-matter insured is reasonably abandoned on account of its actual total loss appearing to be unavoidable, or because it could not be preserved from actual total loss without an expenditure which would exceed its value when the expenditure had been incurred [CITE:2].

This abandonment is based on certain conditions:
- The assured is deprived of the possession of his ship or goods by a peril insured against.
- It is unlikely that he can recover the ship or goods, or the cost of recovering them would exceed their value when recovered [CITE:2].
- In the case of damage to a ship, if the cost of repairing the damage would exceed the value of the ship when repaired [CITE:2].
- In the case of damage to goods, if the cost of repairing the damage and forwarding the goods to their destination would exceed their value on arrival [CITE:2].

The Act provides that where there is a constructive total loss, the assured may either treat the loss as a partial loss or abandon the subject-matter insured to the insurer and treat the loss as if it were an actual total loss [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, under the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (Singapore), when an insurer pays for a partial loss, the rights acquired by the insurer are as follows:

1. **Subrogation**: The insurer becomes subrogated to all the rights and remedies of the assured in and in respect of the subject-matter insured as from the time of the casualty causing the loss, in so far as the assured has been indemnified by such payment for the loss [CITE:1].

2. **No Title to Subject-Matter**: The insurer does not acquire any title to the subject-matter insured, or such part of it as may remain, after paying for a partial loss [CITE:1].

3. **Liability for Successive Losses**: Unless the policy otherwise provides, the insurer is liable for successive losses, even though the total amount of such losses may exceed the sum insured [CITE:4].

4. **Measure of Indemnity**: The measure of indemnity for a partial loss is determined by the provisions of the policy, and may include the reasonable cost of repairs, reasonable depreciation, and other expenses incurred for the safety or preservation of the subject-matter insured [CITE:13, CITE:70].

5. **Right of Contribution**: If the assured is over-insured by double insurance, each insurer is bound to contribute rateably to the loss in proportion to the amount for which they are liable under their contract [CITE:6].

It is important to note that the specific rights and liabilities of the insurer after paying for a partial loss are subject to the terms and conditions of the insurance policy, as well as the provisions of the Marine Insurance Act 1906.

As at 2026-11-06, it is generally not legal to ride an e-scooter on the road in Singapore. As at 2026-11-06, a person holding a valid foreign driving licence may drive in Singapore for a period of 12 months starting from the date of their last entry into Singapore, provided they do not hold a Singapore citizenship or permanent residency, and they are not a work pass driver [CITE:1]. This period is subject to the provisions of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (Singapore) and any amendments or subsidiary legislation in force at the time.

As at 2026-11-06, a child born in Singapore but not a citizen of Singapore at the time of birth is deemed to be issued with a special pass authorising him or her to remain in Singapore [CITE:1]. Therefore, the baby is allowed to stay in Singapore initially for 42 days from the date of birth, with the possibility of extension.

As at 2026-11-06, under the Immigration Act 1959, a Singapore citizen does not need a permit or pass to enter Singapore [CITE:1]. The burden of proof that any person is a citizen of Singapore lies upon that person [CITE:1]. This means that the individual seeking entry must provide evidence of their citizenship to immigration authorities.

As at 2026-11-06, if you remain in Singapore for up to 90 days after your pass has been cancelled, you may be guilty of an offence under section 15 of the Immigration Act 1959 [CITE:1]. The consequences of this offence include:

- A fine not exceeding $4,000;
- Imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months; or
- Both a fine and imprisonment [CITE:1].

It is important to note that this is a summary of the legal provisions and does not constitute legal advice. If you require further information or assistance, you may consult the Singapore Statutes Online or seek legal advice from a qualified lawyer.

As at 2026-11-06, the law in Singapore regarding the reinstatement of an employee called up for national service is governed by the Enlistment Act 1970, section 21 [CITE:2]. According to this section, every employer who has had a person in their employment for a continuous period of at least 6 months immediately preceding the date on which that person was ordered to perform national service, operationally ready national service, or mobilized service, shall reinstate that person in their employment at the termination of such service.

However, there are exceptions to this requirement. The reinstatement obligation does not apply if the person subject to the Act was called up for full-time service and would have remained in that employment only for an agreed definite or certain period of time had that person not been ordered to perform full-time service [CITE:2(3)]. Additionally, the employer may reinstate the person if they have been required to perform further operationally ready national service under section 118(17) of the Singapore Armed Forces Act 1972 [CITE:2(2)].

It is important to note that the employer is required to reinstate the person in an occupation and under conditions not less favourable than those which would have been applicable to them had they not been in service [CITE:2(4)]. As at 2026-11-06, a Correction Direction under the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act 2019 (Singapore) requires the person to whom it is issued to take specific actions in relation to the communication of a false statement of fact in Singapore. The key elements of a Correction Direction are as follows:

1. **Requirement to Communicate a Correction Notice**: The person must communicate a correction notice in Singapore. This notice must contain either a statement that the subject statement is false or a specified statement of fact, or a reference to a location where the specified statement of fact may be found [CITE:1].

2. **Form and Manner of Communication**: The correction notice must be communicated in the specified form and manner, to a specified person or description of persons, and by the specified time [CITE:1].

3. **Online Location**: The Correction Direction may require the person to communicate the correction notice in a specified online location [CITE:1].

4. **Proximity to False Statement**: The person may be required to place the correction notice in the specified proximity to every copy of the false statement of fact or a substantially similar statement that is communicated by the person in Singapore [CITE:1].

5. **Publication in a Newspaper**: The person may also be required to publish the correction notice in a specified newspaper or other printed publication of Singapore [CITE:1].

6. **Application to Unknown Falsehood**: A person who communicated a false statement of fact in Singapore may be issued a Correction Direction even if the person does not know or has no reason to believe that the statement is false [CITE:1].

7. **Exclusions**: The person does not communicate a statement in Singapore merely by doing any act for the purpose of, or that is incidental to, the provision of internet intermediary services, telecommunication services, services of giving the public access to the internet, or computing resource services [CITE:1].

These requirements are designed to ensure that false statements of fact are corrected and that the public is informed of the inaccuracies in such statements.

2. **Cease Communicating Substantially Similar Statements**: The Direction may also require the person to stop communicating any statement that is substantially similar to the subject statement [CITE:1].

3. **Communicate a Correction Notice**: The Direction may require the person to communicate a correction notice in the specified form and manner to a specified person or description of persons, and by the specified time [CITE:1].

4. **Publish a Correction Notice**: The person may also be required to publish a correction notice in a specified newspaper or other printed publication of Singapore [CITE:1].

5. **Removal of Statement from Online Location**: The Direction may include the removal of the statement from an online location to ensure it is no longer available to end-users in Singapore [CITE:1].

These requirements are part of the measures designed to address the communication of false statements of fact online and to ensure that such statements are corrected or removed where necessary.

As at 2026-11-06, customs in Singapore may open a parcel that someone sends to you from overseas under certain circumstances, as governed by the Customs Act 1960 and other relevant legislation. Here are the key points:

1. **Customs Powers**: Under section 108 of the Customs Act 1960, a proper officer of customs has the power to examine any goods in the course of being imported or exported or intended to be imported or exported. This includes the power to open any package or receptacle [CITE:1].

2. **Reasonable Suspicion**: The examination and search of packages, including parcels, can be conducted if a customs officer reasonably suspects that the article is or contains seizable goods [CITE:6].

3. **Search of Persons and Goods**: Section 109 of the Customs Act 1960 allows customs officers to search the person, goods, and baggage of individuals arriving in Singapore, which could include parcels sent to you from overseas [CITE:12].

4. **Postal Services Act**: The Postal Services Act 1999 also provides for the examination of parcels. For instance, section 39I makes it an offence for a person (not being the intended recipient) to wilfully open or cause to be opened any parcel placed in a public parcel locker, except in accordance with the Act or with authorisation by the Postal Authority [CITE:3].

5. **Postal Authority's Powers**: Section 23R of the Postal Services Act 1999 empowers the Postal Authority to direct the public parcel locker network operator to open and search any public parcel locker, and to detain and open any parcel or other article found in the locker, if there is reason to suspect that it is or may be the subject of, or is or may have been used in, the commission of an offence under the Act [CITE:5].

6. **Other Relevant Legislation**: Other legislation, such as the Trade Marks Act 1998 and the Geographical Indications Act 2014, also provide for the examination of packages, including parcels, if there is a reasonable suspicion that they contain goods liable to be seized under those Acts [CITE:16, CITE:9].

In summary, customs in Singapore can open a parcel sent to you from overseas if they have reasonable grounds to suspect that the contents may be subject to seizure or if it is necessary for the purposes of enforcing relevant legislation. It is important to note that these powers are subject to legal constraints and must be exercised in accordance with the law. If you have concerns about the opening of a specific parcel, you may wish to consult a lawyer for advice tailored to your situation.

As at 2026-11-06, the law in Singapore on whether a driver will be blamed for a crash when they swerve in response to another vehicle suddenly putting them in danger is complex and depends on several factors. The following principles are relevant:

1. **Reasonableness of the Action**: A driver's actions must be reasonable considering the exigencies of the situation. If a driver is placed in a dangerous situation due to the negligence of another, their response should not be unreasonable [CITE:1]. This includes considering the surrounding circumstances and the time available to react [CITE:1].

2. **The "Agony of the Moment"**: The courts have recognized the "agony of the moment" principle, which allows for a certain latitude in judgment when a person is faced with a sudden emergency not created by their own negligence. This principle means that a person's conduct in such a situation cannot be judged from the standpoint of what would have been reasonable in hindsight [CITE:19].

3. **Contributory Negligence**: If a driver is placed in a position where they must make a split-second decision, they should not be penalized for contributory negligence even if their actions, in hindsight, might seem less prudent. The court should consider the reality of the situation at the moment before impact [CITE:5].

4. **Duty of Care**: A driver has a duty to keep a proper lookout and to exercise caution, especially at intersections and junctions. However, having the right of way does not mean a driver can collide with another road user with immunity [CITE:16].

5. **Hindsight Analysis**: The courts are cautious about using hindsight to assess a driver's actions. A driver's conduct should be evaluated based on what would have been reasonable in the moment of the emergency, not in the calm of hindsight [CITE:19].

In summary, if you swerve in response to another vehicle suddenly putting you in danger and it turns out not to be the best choice, you may not be blamed for the crash if your actions were reasonable in the moment, considering the exigencies of the situation. The courts will consider the "agony of the moment" and whether your actions were reasonable under the circumstances. However, if your actions were found to be unreasonable or if you were contributorily negligent, you might be held partially liable for the crash. It is important to note that each case is fact-specific, and the outcome can vary based on the particular circumstances of the incident.

4. **Discount for Investment Risk and Contingencies**: A discount is applied to the multiplier to account for the putative investment risk associated with the accelerated receipt of future income as a lump sum, as well as contingencies such as mortality and other considerations affecting life expectancy [CITE:19].

5. **Consideration of the Plaintiff's Competitive Position**: The court considers whether the plaintiff's competitive position in the labor market has been weakened due to the injury, which may affect their ability to secure employment or earn an equally well-paid job [CITE:11, 16].

As at 2026-11-06, if you become the lawful holder of the bill of lading for goods shipped to Singapore, you may have the right to sue the carrier under certain circumstances. The rights and liabilities under the contract of carriage are governed by the relevant provisions of the Bills of Lading Act 1992 [CITE:2], the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1972 [CITE:4, CITE:14], and the Sale of Goods Act 1979 [CITE:5, CITE:16].

Under the Bills of Lading Act 1992, section 2 provides that a person who becomes the lawful holder of a bill of lading has transferred to and vested in him all rights of suit under the contract of carriage as if he had been a party to that contract [CITE:2]. This means that if you are the lawful holder of the bill of lading, you may have the right to sue the carrier for any breach of the contract of carriage.

The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1972 governs the carriage contract for goods by sea. It sets out the responsibilities and liabilities of the carrier, including the duty to exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy and to properly load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for, and discharge the goods carried [CITE:14]. The Act also contains provisions regarding the limitation of liability of the carrier [CITE:8].

The Sale of Goods Act 1979 is relevant in cases where the goods are sold and the contract of carriage is part of the transaction. It provides that where goods are shipped, and by the bill of lading the goods are deliverable to the order of the seller or his agent, the seller is prima facie to be taken to reserve the right of disposal [CITE:5]. This may affect your rights as the holder of the bill of lading.

The international rules that may govern the carriage contract include the Hague-Visby Rules, which are incorporated into the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1972 [CITE:14]. These rules set out the responsibilities and liabilities of the carrier and the rights of the shipper and the consignee.

In summary, as the lawful holder of the bill of lading, you may have the right to sue the carrier for breaches of the contract of carriage, and the carriage contract is governed by the relevant provisions of the Bills of Lading Act 1992, the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1972, and the Sale of Goods Act 1979, as well as the international rules such as the Hague-Visby Rules.

As at 2026-11-06, vehicles in Singapore are required to carry third-party insurance to protect against liabilities arising from accidents caused by the use of the vehicle. This requirement is established under the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960 [CITE:9]. The Act is designed to ensure that victims of road accidents are compensated for their losses, even if the at-fault driver cannot be traced or is unable to pay.

In the case of Man Mohan Singh v Dilveer Singh Gill [2007] SGHC 149, the claim was defended by Zurich Insurance (Singapore) Pte Ltd, the motor insurer of the driver involved in the accident. This occurred because the driver, Dilveer Singh Gill, could not be traced after the accident. When a driver is at fault in an accident and cannot be found, the claim is typically made against the driver's insurance company, provided that the driver had a valid insurance policy in place at the time of the accident.

The insurance company, in this case Zurich Insurance, is required to defend the claim and pay any damages awarded to the victims, up to the limits of the policy. This is in accordance with the provisions of the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960, which mandates that insurers must satisfy judgments against persons insured in respect of third-party risks [CITE:9]. Thus, when the driver is untraceable or unable to pay, the insurance company steps in to fulfill the obligations under the policy.

Under the Maritime Conventions Act 1911 (Cap. IA3, 2004 Rev Ed), when both sides are at fault in a collision, the liability to make good the damage or loss is in proportion to the degree in which each ship was in fault [Source 4]. This means that if two ships are involved in a collision and both are found to be at fault, the liability for the resulting damage will be divided according to the extent of each ship's fault.

In the case of Christian Joachim Pollmann v Ye Xianrong [2017] SGHC 229, the doctrine of contributory negligence is relevant when considering the effect of an injured person's own fault on a personal injury claim. The doctrine of contributory negligence is discussed comprehensively in Asnah bte Ab Rahman v Li Jianlin [2016] 2 SLR 944 [Source 1]. Put simply, a victim of a negligent act is said to have contributed to his own injuries if he ought to have objectively foreseen that his failure to act prudently could result in hurting himself and failed to take reasonable care to guard against that foreseeable harm [Source 1].

In the Pollmann case, the defendant raised the defence of contributory negligence, arguing that the plaintiff contributed to the collision by suddenly swerving to the right and into the defendant's path. However, the court held that the plaintiff did not contribute to his own injuries and that the defendant was 100% liable for the plaintiff's injuries [Source 2]. This decision indicates that in Singapore, the burden of proving contributory negligence lies with the defendant, and the standard of proof is on the balance of probabilities [Source 1].

Therefore, when both sides are at fault, liability is shared according to the degree of fault under the Maritime Conventions Act, and an injured person's own fault can affect a personal injury claim if the defendant can prove contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff.
